answer.query: What can an employee do if they believe they have been unfairly dismissed?
answer.answer: If an employee believes they have been unfairly dismissed, they may make representations in writing to the Director General to be reinstated in their former employment [1]. These representations can be filed at the office of the Director General nearest to the place of employment from which the employee was dismissed [1].

answer.query: Can a dismissed employee claim for compensation or other related claims when filing a case under Section 20 of the IRA 1967?
answer.answer:
Yes, a dismissed employee can claim for compensation or other related claims when filing a case under Section 20 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967. The compensation may include backwages, but there are limits on the amount [1]. 

Backwages, if awarded, should not exceed twenty-four months’ backwages from the date of dismissal based on the last-drawn salary of the person who has been dismissed without just cause or excuse [1]. For a probationer, the backwages given shall not exceed twelve months’ backwages from the date of dismissal based on his last-drawn salary [1].

Additionally, if the employee earned money after dismissal, a percentage of such earnings, to be decided by the Court, shall be deducted from the backwages given [1]. However, any relief given shall not include any compensation for loss of future earnings [1]. Also, any relief given shall take into account contributory misconduct of the workman [1].

answer.query: How to obtain cognizance for a Collective Agreement?
answer.answer:
To obtain cognizance for a Collective Agreement, a signed copy of the agreement must be jointly deposited by the parties with the Registrar within one month from the date on which the agreement has been entered into [1]. The Registrar will then bring it to the notice of the Court for its cognizance [1].

answer.query: What are the implications for a Collective Agreement that has been given cognizance by the Industrial Court?
answer.answer:
A Collective Agreement that has been given cognizance by the Industrial Court is deemed to be an award and is binding on the parties to the agreement, including all members of a trade union of employers and their successors, assignees, or transferees, as well as all workmen employed in the undertaking or part of the undertaking to which the agreement relates [1]. 

If any term of such an award or collective agreement is not complied with, any trade union or person bound by the award or agreement may lodge a complaint with the Court in writing [2]. 

If any question arises regarding the interpretation of the award or collective agreement, the Minister may refer the question to the Court, or any party bound by the award or agreement may apply to the Court for a decision on the question [3]. 

Additionally, the Industrial Court may refuse to take cognizance of a collective agreement if it does not comply with specific requirements, or it may require amendments to parts of the agreement that do not comply with those requirements before taking cognizance of it [4]. 

Furthermore, terms or conditions of service provided for in such a collective agreement or award are not subject to the provisions of Part XII of the Employment Act 1955, as long as the agreement or award remains in force [5].

answer.answer: To qualify for 7 days of paid paternity leave, a married male employee must have been employed by the same employer for at least twelve months immediately before the commencement of such paternity leave [1]. If a female employee miscarries after 22 weeks of pregnancy, her husband may be eligible for 7 days of paid paternity leave if he meets all other criteria. The law states that a married male employee is entitled to a paid paternity leave at his ordinary rate of pay for a period of seven consecutive days in respect of each confinement [1]. 

To be eligible for paternity leave, the male employee must have been employed by the same employer at least twelve months immediately before the commencement of such paternity leave, and he must have notified his employer of the pregnancy of his spouse at least thirty days from the expected confinement or as early as possible after the birth [2].

However, it is reasonable to infer that a miscarriage at this stage of pregnancy may be considered a confinement, as it involves a significant medical event similar to childbirth. If this is the case, then the husband would be eligible for the 7 days of paid paternity leave, provided he meets the other conditions outlined in the law.

answer.query: Company A practices an 8-hour workday with 6 working days per week. To implement the reduction of working hours from 48 hours per week to 45 hours per week, can Company A reduce the working days to 5 days per week and extend the daily working hours to 9 hours?
answer.answer:
Under Malaysian employment law, an employee cannot be required to work more than eight hours in one day, except under specific conditions outlined in the law [1]. If an employer and employee agree in their contract of service that the number of hours of work on one or more days of the week is less than eight, the limit of eight hours may be exceeded on the remaining days of the week, but no employee shall be required to work for more than nine hours in one day or forty-five hours in one week [1].

If Company A wants to reduce the working hours from 48 hours per week to 45 hours per week, it could potentially reduce the working days to five days per week and extend the daily working hours to nine hours, provided that the total weekly hours do not exceed forty-five hours and that no single day exceeds nine hours of work [1]. This would be permissible under the law, as long as the agreement between the employer and employee allows for such a change in the contract of service.

answer.query: If an employer practicing a 6-day workweek reduces the daily working hours from 8 hours to 7.5 hours to meet the 45-hour weekly working requirement, how will the calculation of Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) and Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for overtime payment purposes be affected?
answer.answer:
If an employer reduces daily working hours from 8 hours to 7.5 hours to meet the 45-hour weekly working requirement, the Ordinary Rate of Pay (ORP) and Hourly Rate of Pay (HRP) for overtime payment purposes will be calculated based on the new normal hours of work [1][2][3][4][5].

For an employee on a monthly rate of pay, the ORP would be calculated using the formula: monthly rate of pay / 26 [4]. This ORP would then be divided by the new normal hours of work (7.5 hours per day) to determine the HRP [5].

For an employee on a weekly rate of pay, the ORP would be calculated using the formula: weekly rate of pay / 6 [2]. This ORP would then be divided by the new normal hours of work (7.5 hours per day) to determine the HRP [5].

For an employee on a daily or hourly rate of pay or on piece rates, the ORP would be calculated by dividing the total wages earned by the employee during the preceding wage period (excluding any payment made under an approved incentive payment scheme or for work done on any rest day, any gazetted public holiday granted by the employer under the contract of service or any day substituted for the gazetted public holiday) by the actual number of days the employee had worked during that wage period (excluding any rest day, any gazetted public holiday or any paid holiday substituted for the gazetted public holiday) [3]. This ORP would then be divided by the new normal hours of work (7.5 hours per day) to determine the HRP [5].

The normal hours of work for the purposes of calculating overtime is the number of hours of work as agreed between an employer and an employee in the contract of service to be the usual hours of work per day and such hours of work shall not exceed the limits of hours prescribed in subsection (1) [1].

answer.query: What elements can prove that someone is an employee in the absence of a written employment contract?
answer.answer:
In the absence of a written employment contract, the following elements can be used to prove that someone is an employee:

- If their manner of work is subject to the control or direction of another person [1].
- If their hours of work are subject to the control or direction of another person [1].
- If they are provided with tools, materials, or equipment by another person to execute work [1].
- If their work constitutes an integral part of another person’s business [1].
- If their work is performed solely for the benefit of another person [1].
- If payment is made to them in return for work done by them at regular intervals and such payment constitutes the majority of their income [1].

answer.query: I got fired an hour before work ended without any warning letter or termination letter. My boss told me not to come to work and that he'll pay me a month's worth of salary later, and asked me to give him a resignation letter. What do I do?

If you were fired without any warning or termination letter, and your employer told you not to come to work and offered to pay you a month's worth of salary later, you may be entitled to certain payments depending on the circumstances [1]. If your employer is asking you to provide a resignation letter, this may be an attempt to frame the termination as your own choice rather than their decision. You should ensure that any payment you receive is in accordance with the law, and that you are not being asked to resign under pressure or without proper compensation [1].

answer.query: In my offer letter I need to give 1 month notice. But I haven't gotten my salary for 3 months, which led me to quit without notice. Do my employers still need to pay me my 3 months salary, or do I need to pay my employers a month salary as compensation stated in the offer letter?
answer.answer:
If you quit without giving notice, your employer is still required to pay you the wages earned up to the day before your termination, less any deductions they are entitled to make [1][2]. This means that your employer must pay you the salary for the three months you worked, less any lawful deductions.

However, if your offer letter states that you need to give one month's notice and you did not give it, your employer may be entitled to deduct from your final wages an amount equivalent to one month's salary as compensation for the notice period [3]. This deduction would be based on the terms of your contract or the applicable law in your region.

In Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, the employer must pay your wages not later than the third day after the termination of your contract [1]. In Sabah, the same rule applies [2]. In Sarawak, the law has been amended, and wages should be paid not later than the seventh day after the last day of the wage period [4].

answer.query: My supervisor said I am going to be sacked and this month is my last month due to poor performance. There is no written contract between me and my workplace (a minimart) and my only proof of employment was some WhatsApp messages that I lost. What should I do now?
answer.answer:
Based on the information provided, the following points may be relevant to your situation:

1. If your employment was for a period exceeding one month or for the performance of a specified piece of work that would reasonably take more than one month to complete, then your contract should have been in writing [1]. However, since you mentioned there is no written contract, it may be that your employment falls under an oral agreement or is considered casual or short-term.

2. If your employer is terminating your contract due to poor performance, they must follow the procedures outlined in the relevant employment laws. In Peninsular Malaysia and Labuan, if an employer terminates an employee due to misconduct, they must conduct due inquiry before taking any action [2]. However, poor performance may not necessarily be considered misconduct unless it is inconsistent with the conditions of your service.

3. If you feel that your termination is unjust or you believe your employer is not following the proper procedures, you may want to seek further information or assistance from local labor authorities or legal professionals who can guide you on your rights and options [2].

4. In Sabah, similar provisions apply regarding termination for special reasons, including due inquiry and the types of punishments that can be imposed [3]. However, since your workplace is a minimart, it is likely located in Peninsular Malaysia or Labuan, not Sabah.

5. If you are a domestic employee, your contract may be terminated by either party with fourteen days' notice or by paying an indemnity equivalent to fourteen days' wages [4]. However, this provision applies specifically to domestic employees, and it is unclear if you fall into this category.

6. If you or your dependants are immediately threatened by danger to the person by violence or disease, you may terminate your contract without notice [5]. However, this does not seem to apply to your situation as it is related to threats to your person, not poor performance.

Since you do not have a written contract and have lost your WhatsApp messages, it may be difficult to prove your employment relationship. You may want to gather any other evidence of your employment, such as pay slips, work schedules, or witness statements. If you believe your termination is unfair or unlawful, you may need to consult with a legal professional or labor authority for further assistance.

answer.query: When is the deadline for wage payment?
answer.answer: The deadline for wage payment is not later than the seventh day after the last day of any wage period [1]. However, wages for work done on a rest day, gazette public holiday, or overtime should be paid not later than the last day of the next wage period [2]. If an employee's contract of service terminates normally, wages earned but not yet paid should be given not later than the day the contract terminates [3]. If an employee terminates the contract without notice, wages up to the day before termination should be paid not later than the third day after the termination [4]. A wage period specified in the contract of service cannot exceed one month [5].

answer.query: When can maternity leave be taken?
answer.answer:
Maternity leave can be taken starting no earlier than thirty days before the confinement of a female employee and no later than the day immediately following her confinement [1]. However, if a medical officer or a registered medical practitioner appointed by the employer certifies that the female employee is unable to perform her duties due to her advanced state of pregnancy, she may start her maternity leave at any time during a period of fourteen days before her confinement [1].

If a female employee starts her maternity leave earlier than thirty days before her confinement, the days she abstains from work in excess of that period will not be treated as maternity leave, and she will not be entitled to any maternity allowance for those days [2].

Additionally, a female employee may, with the consent of her employer, commence work at any time during the eligible period if she has been certified fit to resume work by a registered medical practitioner [3]. The "eligible period" is defined as a period of maternity leave of not less than ninety-eight consecutive days [4]. 

If an employee is on paid annual leave and becomes entitled to maternity leave during that time, the maternity leave will be granted, and the annual leave will be deemed not to have been taken for the days of maternity leave [5]. 

For the purposes of this section, "children" means all natural children, irrespective of age [6].

answer.answer:

answer.query: How many days of annual leave is an employee entitled to?
answer.answer:
An employee is entitled to paid annual leave based on the length of their continuous service with the same employer. If they have been employed for less than two years, they are entitled to eight days of annual leave for every twelve months of service. If they have been employed for two years or more but less than five years, they are entitled to twelve days of annual leave for every twelve months of service. If they have been employed for five years or more, they are entitled to sixteen days of annual leave for every twelve months of service [1]. 

If an employee has not completed twelve months of continuous service with the same employer during the year in which their contract of service terminates, their entitlement to paid annual leave shall be in direct proportion to the number of completed months of service [1]. 

Additionally, any fraction of a day of annual leave calculated which is less than one-half of a day shall be disregarded, and where the fraction of a day is one-half or more it shall be deemed to be one day [1]. 

It is also important to note that if an employee absents themselves from work without the permission of their employer and without reasonable excuse for more than ten percent of the working days during the twelve months of continuous service in respect of which their entitlement to such leave accrues, they shall not be entitled to such leave [1].

answer.query: What is the new entitlement for sick leave and hospitalisation leave effective from 1 May 2025?
answer.answer:
The new entitlement for sick leave and hospitalisation leave effective from 1 May 2025 is that an employee is entitled to paid sick leave after examination by a registered medical practitioner appointed by the employer or another registered medical practitioner or a medical officer if the employer has not appointed one or if it is not obtainable within a reasonable time or distance [1]. 

For sick leave where no hospitalization is necessary, the entitlement is fourteen days in the aggregate in each calendar year if the employee has been employed for less than two years, eighteen days if employed for two years or more but less than five years, and twenty-two days if employed for five years or more [1].

For hospitalisation leave, an employee is entitled to sixty days in the aggregate in each calendar year if hospitalisation is necessary, as certified by a registered medical practitioner or medical officer [1]. However, the total number of days of paid sick leave in a calendar year which an employee is entitled to under this section shall be sixty days in the aggregate [1].

Additionally, if an employee is certified by a registered medical practitioner or medical officer to be ill enough to need to be hospitalised but is not hospitalised for any reason, the employee shall be deemed to be hospitalised for the purposes of this section [1].

answer.query: What is the limit for overtime work?
answer.answer:
The limit for overtime work in Sarawak is determined by the average number of hours worked over any period of three weeks, or over any period exceeding three weeks as may be approved by the Director, which should not exceed forty-five hours per week [1][2]. 

Additionally, "overtime" is defined as the number of hours of work carried out in excess of the normal hours of work per day, or if any work is carried out after the spread over period of ten hours, the whole period beginning from the time that such spread over period ends up to the time that the employee ceases work for the day [3].

answer.query: How to file a complaint?
answer.answer:
To file a complaint, you can lodge it in writing with the appropriate authority, depending on the nature of the issue. If the complaint is about a contravention of specific sections (such as section 4, 5, or 7 of the Industrial Relations Act 1967), it should be lodged with the Director General, detailing all the facts and circumstances of the complaint [1].

If the complaint is about non-compliance with an award or collective agreement, it should be lodged with the Industrial Court in writing by any trade union or person bound by such award or agreement [2].

In Sarawak, if the complaint relates to the Labour Ordinance, the procedure involves presenting a written statement of the complaint and the remedy sought to the Director. The Director will then examine the complainant on oath or affirmation and may summon the person complained against for further inquiry [3]. However, note that this section has been amended, and the current procedure may involve sections 8a and 19a of the Ordinance [4].

The Cap. 76 text retrieved here predates that substitution, so where it reads "worker" or "domestic servant" the operative term is now "employee" or "domestic employee". The wording is not rewritten in the source text, so that the user can still verify it against the published Ordinance.

The text held here incorporates amendments only up to 31 July 2006. Act A1754 has been in force since 1 May 2025, so every provision it amends still carries pre-amendment wording in this document. Those sections are marked status: superseded at chunk level and carry an amended_by link to the operative A1754 provision.
